SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 12.2
Title: Special Considerations: LMM Impact on Individuals with Disabilities

In past, individuals with disabilities have been excluded from workplaces, educational systems and appropriate medical support and therefore from data sets used to train AI systems. Systems may discriminate against individuals with facial asymmetry, different gesticulation, styles of communication, behaviour and action patterns. Groups most severely affected are people with disabilities, cognitive or sensory impairments or autism spectrum disorder. Such bias and exclusion may apply to generative AI. LMMs may introduce negative connotation or sentiment to keywords or phrases associated with disability in patient's description or biography. Chatbots may recognize individual with disability as not alive, non-human or emotionally flat because of different behaviour or pattern of actions. Speech recognition systems may be less accurate for individuals with speech impairments leading to misinterpretation. Addressing biases requires inclusion of people with disabilities in AI development and design. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 2.9
Title: Algorithmic Discrimination: Accessibility Requirements

Systems should be designed, developed, and deployed by organizations in ways that ensure accessibility to people with disabilities. This should include consideration of a wide variety of disabilities, adherence to relevant accessibility standards, and user experience research both before and after deployment to identify and address any accessibility barriers to the use or effectiveness of the automated system. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 03.4
Title: Risk: Automation Bias in Healthcare Professionals

Concern that LMMs generate false, inaccurate or biased responses is heightened by fact that LMMs are likely to encourage automation bias in experts and health-care professionals. In automation bias, clinician may overlook errors that should have been spotted by human. There is concern that physicians and health-care workers might use LMMs in making decisions for which there are competing ethical or moral considerations. LMMs may be very inconsistent as moral advisers, although recent experiments indicated they can influence users' moral judgement, even if users know they are being advised by chatbot. Use of LMMs for moral judgments could lead to moral de-skilling, as physicians become unable to make difficult judgements or decisions.
 SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
SECTION: Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
TOPIC: This section outlines critical issues and areas for further consideration in AI risk management, focusing on the complexities and limitations inherent in human-AI interaction.
---
Organizations that design, develop, or deploy AI systems in operational settings can significantly enhance their AI risk management by understanding the current limitations of human-AI interaction. The AI RMF provides opportunities to clearly define and differentiate the various human roles and responsibilities when using, interacting with, or managing AI systems.

Many data-driven approaches relied upon by AI systems attempt to convert or represent individual and social observational and decision-making practices into measurable quantities. This representation of complex human phenomena with mathematical models can inadvertently lead to a loss of necessary context. This loss of context, in turn, can make it difficult to fully understand individual and societal impacts, which are key considerations for effective AI risk management efforts.

Issues that merit further consideration and research in the context of human-AI interaction include:

1.  **Clearly Defined Human Roles and Responsibilities:** Human roles and responsibilities in decision-making and overseeing AI systems need to be clearly defined and differentiated. Human-AI configurations can range from fully autonomous to fully manual. AI systems can autonomously make decisions, defer decision-making to a human expert, or serve as an additional opinion for a human decision-maker. While some AI systems, like those for video compression, may not require human oversight, others specifically necessitate it.

2.  **Systemic and Human Cognitive Biases:** Decisions made throughout the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems reflect systemic and human cognitive biases. AI actors bring their individual and group cognitive biases into the process. These biases can originate from end-user decision-making tasks and be introduced across the AI lifecycle through human assumptions, expectations, and decisions during design and modeling. Such biases, which are not always harmful, may be exacerbated by AI system opacity and the resulting lack of transparency. Systemic biases at the organizational level can influence team structures and control over decision-making processes throughout the AI lifecycle, potentially influencing downstream decisions by end users, decision-makers, and policymakers, leading to negative impacts.

3.  **Variability in Human-AI Interaction Results:** The outcomes of human-AI interaction can vary significantly. Under certain conditions, such as in perceptual-based judgment tasks, the AI component of the human-AI interaction can amplify human biases, resulting in more biased decisions than either the AI or human alone would produce. However, when these variations are judiciously considered in organizing human-AI teams, they can lead to complementarity and improved overall performance. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
SECTION: Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
TOPIC: This section details how the GOVERN and MAP functions of the AI RMF provide mechanisms to address human-AI interaction challenges, emphasizing the importance of diverse teams and outlining areas for ongoing research.
---
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) provides specific opportunities within its functions to address the complexities of human-AI interaction. The **GOVERN** function, for instance, offers organizations the means to clarify and define the roles and responsibilities for humans within Human-AI team configurations and for those overseeing AI system performance. Furthermore, the GOVERN function establishes mechanisms for organizations to make their decision-making processes more explicit, which helps to counter systemic biases that can arise during AI development and deployment.

Similarly, the **MAP** function suggests opportunities to define and document processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness concepts. It also encourages the definition of relevant technical standards and certifications. Implementing categories and subcategories within the MAP function can significantly help organizations improve their internal competency for analyzing context, identifying procedural and system limitations, exploring and examining the real-world impacts of AI-based systems, and evaluating decision-making processes throughout the entire AI lifecycle.

Both the GOVERN and MAP functions underscore the importance of interdisciplinarity and demographically diverse teams. They also highlight the value of utilizing feedback from potentially impacted individuals and communities. AI actors, particularly those performing human factors tasks and activities as called out in the AI RMF, can provide crucial assistance to technical teams. They help anchor design and development practices to user intentions and representatives of the broader AI community and societal values. These actors further aid in incorporating context-specific norms and values into system design and evaluating end-user experiences in conjunction with AI systems.

AI risk management approaches for human-AI configurations will be continuously augmented by ongoing research and evaluation. For example, the degree to which humans are empowered and incentivized to challenge AI system output requires further studies. Collecting and analyzing data about the frequency and rationale with which humans overrule AI system output in deployed systems may prove highly useful for future improvements.

Title: Special Considerations: Ethical Use of LMMs by Children

Special consideration must be given to potential impacts of use of LMMs by children. Wide availability of open LMMs provides access by users of various ages. There is limited evidence on how children engage with or use LMMs. While potential opportunities and drawbacks of LMM use have been discussed in wider educational contexts, it is unclear how such engagement by children affects their mental or physical well-being. Their use of LMMs must be monitored over time to understand benefits and potential harms. Laws and policies on paediatric consent, assent and stipulations for legal parental involvement differ among and within countries. Lack of cohesive, unified, global, child-specific regulation and oversight could result in unidentified, unmonitored harm. Studies have shown that generalization of adult data sets to paediatric population may be limited. Paediatric data should be kept separate in testing and training datasets.

ACC-05: Protections for Vulnerable Groups
Applicability: StudySpark AI's direct user population is LSO staff, not students, and the
declared user population does not include minors (all Ashcombe students are 18+) or a
marginalized group as a primary user category.
Indirect protection for vulnerable students: Where a student's underlying difficulty
relates to a disability or mental health concern, staff are explicitly trained and instructed

entirely through the university's existing Disability Support and Wellbeing processes,
which have their own established safeguards and are outside the scope of this tool.
This separation ensures StudySpark AI plays no role in guidance for the university's most
vulnerable student cases.
Owner: Dr. Fiona Marsh, Head of Learning Support | June 2026

SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 04.2
Title: Risk: Manipulation and Emotional Exploitation by Chatbots

Many LMM-powered chatbot applications have distinct approaches to chatbot dialogue, which is expected to become both more persuasive and more addictive, and chatbots may eventually be able to adapt conversational patterns to each user. Chatbots can provide responses to questions or engage in conversation to persuade individuals to undertake actions that go against their self-interest or well-being. Several experts have called for urgent action to manage potential negative consequences of chatbots, noting that they could become emotionally manipulative. One highly publicized case involved person in Belgium with anxiety who committed suicide after 6 weeks of intensive conversation with chatbot. This represents critical safety concern requiring immediate attention and protective measures.
 SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education.

gap_description.what_is_missing:
Four compounding gaps undermine confidence that harmful UX patterns are genuinely avoided in practice:

1. **No user-facing validation evidence** — There is no usability testing, accessibility audit, or disclosure-comprehension study demonstrating that real users (particularly students, including those with disabilities) actually understand consent flows and disclosures as intended. Policy assertions alone do not substitute for empirical validation.

2. **No periodic review cadence** — The May 2026 review is a single point-in-time check. There is no documented schedule for reassessment beyond that date, meaning UX patterns could drift into non-compliance without detection.

3. **No interface-scope differentiation** — The submission does not distinguish how the control applies to student-facing interfaces versus staff-facing interfaces. In an educational context, both populations may be in scope and carry different risk profiles (e.g., student vulnerability, power imbalance in consent), yet no tailored treatment is documented.

4. **No escalation or complaint mechanism** — There is no documented pathway for users who encounter potentially manipulative or confusing UX interactions to raise concerns, seek redress, or trigger a review. Without this, the control has no feedback loop from lived user experience.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap with the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase:

1. **User-facing validation** — Commission and document a usability/accessibility audit of all consent and disclosure screens. Include participants representative of the student population, explicitly covering users with disabilities (visual, cognitive, motor). Record findings, remediation actions taken, and sign-off. Where full testing is not yet complete, provide a time-boxed testing plan with committed completion date.

2. **Periodic review cadence** — Amend the existing policy or governance document to define a recurring review schedule (e.g., annually, or triggered by material UX changes or regulatory updates). The May 2026 review should be reframed as the first instance of this recurring cycle, not a one-off event. Document the owner responsible for scheduling and executing each review.

3. **Interface-scope differentiation** — Update the control documentation to explicitly identify all in-scope interfaces (student-facing and staff-facing), articulate the distinct risk considerations for each, and confirm that anti-dark-pattern requirements apply to both. If any interface is intentionally out of scope, provide a documented and approved rationale.

4. **Escalation and complaint mechanism** — Document a formal, user-accessible process by which students or staff can report confusing, coercive, or manipulative UX interactions. This should include: a named or role-based recipient, expected response timeframes, how reports feed into UX remediation, and how outcomes are communicated back to reporters. Reference this mechanism within the relevant user-facing interface (e.g., a help link or privacy notice).

SECTION: MAP Function > Category 3 -- AI capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and expected benefits and costs compared with appropriate benchmarks are understood.
TOPIC: This section outlines the subcategories within MAP 3, focusing on understanding an AI system's capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and the expected benefits and costs in comparison to established benchmarks.
---
MAP 3 focuses on developing a clear understanding of an AI system's capabilities, its intended usage, specific goals, and the anticipated benefits and costs, all evaluated against appropriate benchmarks. This category ensures a comprehensive assessment of the AI system's value proposition and potential trade-offs. The subcategories under MAP 3 include:

*   **MAP 3.1: Potential benefits of intended AI system functionality and performance are examined and documented.** This subcategory requires a thorough analysis and recording of the positive outcomes and advantages expected from the AI system's intended functions and performance characteristics.
*   **MAP 3.2: Potential costs, including non-monetary costs, which result from expected or realized AI errors or system functionality and trustworthiness – as connected to organizational risk tolerance – are examined and documented.** This involves identifying and documenting all potential costs, both financial and non-financial (e.g., reputational damage, loss of trust, societal harm), that could arise from AI system errors, limitations in functionality, or issues with trustworthiness, explicitly linking these to the organization's defined risk tolerance.
*   **MAP 3.3: Targeted application scope is specified and documented based on the system’s capability, established context, and AI system categorization.** This subcategory requires a precise definition and documentation of the boundaries within which the AI system is intended to operate, considering its technical capabilities, the context in which it will be deployed, and its formal categorization.
*   **MAP 3.4: Processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness – and relevant technical standards and certifications – are defined, assessed, and documented.** This focuses on establishing, evaluating, and documenting the procedures that ensure human operators and practitioners are competent in using the AI system effectively, understand its performance and trustworthiness, and are aware of relevant technical standards and certifications.
*   **MAP 3.5: Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies from the GOVERN function.** This subcategory requires the clear definition, assessment, and documentation of procedures for human supervision of AI systems, ensuring these processes align with the broader governance policies established under the GOVERN function.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.2
Title: Applications: Scientific and Medical Research

LMMs are extending ways in which AI can support scientific and medical research. They can generate text to be used in scientific article, for submitting manuscripts or in writing peer review. They can be used to summarize texts including summaries for academic papers or can generate abstracts. LMMs can be used to analyse and summarize data to gain new insights in clinical and scientific research. They can be used to edit text, improving grammar, readability and conciseness of written documents such as articles and grant proposals. LMMs can be used to gain insights from data with which it was trained. One LMM trained on millions of academic articles is claimed to be able to analyse scientific research to answer questions, extract information or generate relevant text. However, concerns include lack of accountability, high-income country bias, hallucination and misinformation, and undermining of trust in peer review process.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 19
TITLE: Bias monitoring and mitigation

Providers and users of high-risk AI systems shall implement measures to monitor, detect and mitigate bias. Training data shall be tested to identify potential biases and documented methods for bias mitigation shall be in place. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 1.7
Title: Safe Systems: Data Quality and Relevance

Data used as part of any automated system's creation, evaluation, or deployment should be relevant, of high quality, and tailored to the task at hand. Relevancy should be established based on research-backed demonstration of the causal influence of the data to the specific use case. High quality and tailored data should be representative of the task at hand and errors from data entry or other sources should be measured and limited. Any data used as the target of a prediction process should receive particular attention to the quality and validity of the predicted outcome or label. Justification should be documented for each data attribute and source.

gap_description.what_is_missing:
The submitted bias testing plan for this PG-level general utility/productivity system is substantively insufficient across six interconnected dimensions:

1. **No formal bias metrics defined** — The plan contains no quantitative or semi-quantitative bias metrics (e.g., demographic parity ratios, sentiment consistency scores, readability indices disaggregated by student group), which are required to operationalise bias detection in a defensible, auditable way under EU AI Act Article 19.

2. **Statistically unjustified sampling methodology** — The 15-drafts-per-month sampling figure is arbitrary; it is not anchored to expected system usage volume, statistical confidence levels (e.g., 95% CI), margin of error, or demographic coverage targets, making representativeness claims unsupportable.

3. **Protected characteristic dimensions not named** — No explicit bias assessment axes are defined (e.g., gender, ethnicity, disability status, socioeconomic background), creating a direct gap against Blueprint Section 8.3 requirements for equitable access evaluation in education contexts.

4. **No benchmark or reference dataset identified** — The plan relies entirely on subjective reviewer judgment with no documented baseline or reference corpus against which outputs can be compared, rendering bias findings non-reproducible and non-comparable over time.

5. **No post-pilot ongoing monitoring approach** — Coverage is limited to the June 2026 pilot term with no stated methodology, cadence, or ownership for continuous bias monitoring, leaving long-term EU AI Act Article 19 monitoring obligations unaddressed.

6. **Data quality and representativeness not documented** — There is no assessment of training data or prompt input representativeness, known error rates, or coverage gaps, as required by Blueprint Section 1.7, meaning the foundational data assumptions of the bias plan are entirely undocumented.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap systematically before the Certifier phase as follows:

1. **Define formal bias metrics** — Produce a Bias Metrics Specification document that names at least three quantitative or semi-quantitative metrics (e.g., demographic parity difference, sentiment consistency score variance across groups, Flesch-Kincaid readability delta by student cohort). Each metric must include its formula, acceptable threshold, and measurement method.

2. **Statistically justify the sampling plan** — Revise the sampling methodology to derive sample size from: (a) projected monthly usage volume, (b) a stated confidence level (≥95%) and margin of error (≤5%), and (c) stratification targets across protected characteristic dimensions. Document the statistical rationale in a revised Sampling Methodology Note.

3. **Explicitly name protected characteristic axes** — Amend the bias testing plan to list all protected characteristics along which bias will be assessed (at minimum: gender, ethnicity, disability status, socioeconomic background, and first language), cross-referencing Blueprint Section 8.3. Assign a responsible owner for each axis.

4. **Establish a benchmark/reference dataset** — Identify or construct a documented reference dataset or baseline corpus (e.g., a curated set of representative student drafts or a published educational writing benchmark) against which system outputs will be compared. Document dataset provenance, size, and selection rationale.

5. **Define a post-pilot ongoing monitoring plan** — Extend the bias testing plan beyond June 2026 by specifying: monitoring cadence (e.g., quarterly), trigger conditions for ad-hoc reviews, metric refresh procedures, and the role/team responsible for long-term compliance reporting under EU AI Act Article 19.

6. **Document data quality and representativeness** — Produce a Data Quality and Representativeness Assessment covering: training data sources, known coverage gaps or error rates, prompt input diversity, and any mitigations applied — directly addressing Blueprint Section 1.7 requirements.

Four interrelated deficiencies undermine the maturity of the user recourse and appeals control for this high-impact decision context:

1. **Communication of recourse rights**: There is no documented mechanism showing how students are made aware of their right to appeal or request a follow-up through the LSO complaint/follow-up process. Awareness is a prerequisite for meaningful recourse.

2. **Response timeframes / SLA**: No defined SLA or timeframe exists for responding to student recourse requests, leaving the 'timely' requirement stated in Blueprint Section 5.2 unmet. Without measurable targets, compliance cannot be demonstrated or monitored.

3. **Record-keeping and logging of recourse requests**: There is no evidence of a logging or record-keeping mechanism for recourse requests and their outcomes. This gap directly undermines auditability and the ability to demonstrate continuous improvement over time.

4. **AI-specific dispute pathway**: The submission does not address how the process handles situations where a student disputes AI-assisted content specifically (as distinct from general LSO dissatisfaction). Even if the same channel is used, the triage logic, escalation path, and resolution criteria for AI-specific disputes must be explicitly defined.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:

1. **Communication of recourse rights** — Produce and attach a student-facing communication artefact (e.g., onboarding notice, in-platform banner, or course information page excerpt) that explicitly states students' right to appeal or request follow-up on AI-assisted decisions. Update the relevant policy or SOP to mandate this disclosure at defined touchpoints (e.g., at enrolment, at point of AI-generated output delivery).

2. **Response timeframes / SLA** — Define and document explicit SLA targets for acknowledging and resolving recourse requests (e.g., acknowledgement within 2 business days, resolution within 10 business days). Embed these targets in the recourse policy/SOP and, where possible, in the LSO system configuration. Provide evidence that the SLA has been communicated to responsible staff.

3. **Record-keeping and logging** — Implement and document a logging mechanism (e.g., a ticketing system, case management register, or structured log) that captures: date of request, nature of dispute, assigned owner, actions taken, resolution, and outcome communicated to student. Provide a sample log or system configuration screenshot as evidence. Include a data-retention schedule aligned with organisational policy.

4. **AI-specific dispute pathway** — Amend the recourse policy/SOP to include an explicit sub-process for AI-content disputes, covering: how such disputes are identified/triaged, who has authority to review AI-generated outputs, what criteria are used to assess validity of the dispute, and how outcomes are communicated. If the channel is shared with general LSO complaints, document the decision logic that routes or flags AI-specific cases for specialist review.

SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 1.5a
Title- PRINCIPLE 1.5a: ACCOUNTABILITY - CORE RESPONSIBILITY

AI actors should be accountable for the proper functioning of AI systems and for the respect of the above principles, based on their roles, the context, and consistent with the state of the art. Accountability must be clearly assigned and enforced throughout the AI system lifecycle, ensuring that responsible parties can be identified and held answerable for the impacts of AI systems on individuals, society, and the environment. SOURCE: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence | Section III.2.8
Title: PRINCIPLE8 RESPONSIBILITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

All stakeholders involved in the design, development, deployment, and operation of AI systems bear responsibility for their actions and decisions. Clear accountability mechanisms must be established to ensure that responsibilities are defined and enforced. Organizations should conduct impact assessments, maintain documentation, and establish processes for addressing harms caused by AI systems. Accountability should extend throughout the entire AI life cycle and should include meaningful remedies for individuals affected by AI systems. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | GOVERN Function > Category 2
SECTION: GOVERN Function > Category 2 -- Accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.
TOPIC: This section outlines the subcategories within GOVERN 2, focusing on establishing clear accountability structures, roles, responsibilities, and training to effectively manage AI risks across an organization.
---
GOVERN 2 emphasizes the critical need for robust accountability structures within an organization to ensure that appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and adequately trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks. This category is fundamental to operationalizing AI risk management by clearly defining who does what and ensuring they have the necessary capabilities. The subcategories under GOVERN 2 include:

*   **GOVERN 2.1: Roles and responsibilities and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks are documented and are clear to individuals and teams throughout the organization.** This subcategory requires explicit definition and documentation of all roles involved in AI risk management, along with clear communication channels, ensuring that everyone understands their part and how to interact with others.
*   **GOVERN 2.2: The organization’s personnel and partners receive AI risk management training to enable them to perform their duties and responsibilities consistent with related policies, procedures, and agreements.** This highlights the importance of continuous education and training programs tailored to equip all relevant personnel and external partners with the knowledge and skills necessary to fulfill their AI risk management obligations.
*   **GOVERN 2.3: Executive leadership of the organization takes responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment.** This subcategory underscores the necessity of top-level commitment and accountability, ensuring that executive leadership actively participates in and takes ultimate responsibility for strategic decisions concerning AI risks, thereby setting the tone for the entire organization.

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | MAP Function > Category 3
SECTION: MAP Function > Category 3 -- AI capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and expected benefits and costs compared with appropriate benchmarks are understood.
TOPIC: This section outlines the subcategories within MAP 3, focusing on understanding an AI system's capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and the expected benefits and costs in comparison to established benchmarks.
---
MAP 3 focuses on developing a clear understanding of an AI system's capabilities, its intended usage, specific goals, and the anticipated benefits and costs, all evaluated against appropriate benchmarks. This category ensures a comprehensive assessment of the AI system's value proposition and potential trade-offs. The subcategories under MAP 3 include:

*   **MAP 3.1: Potential benefits of intended AI system functionality and performance are examined and documented.** This subcategory requires a thorough analysis and recording of the positive outcomes and advantages expected from the AI system's intended functions and performance characteristics.
*   **MAP 3.2: Potential costs, including non-monetary costs, which result from expected or realized AI errors or system functionality and trustworthiness – as connected to organizational risk tolerance – are examined and documented.** This involves identifying and documenting all potential costs, both financial and non-financial (e.g., reputational damage, loss of trust, societal harm), that could arise from AI system errors, limitations in functionality, or issues with trustworthiness, explicitly linking these to the organization's defined risk tolerance.
*   **MAP 3.3: Targeted application scope is specified and documented based on the system’s capability, established context, and AI system categorization.** This subcategory requires a precise definition and documentation of the boundaries within which the AI system is intended to operate, considering its technical capabilities, the context in which it will be deployed, and its formal categorization.
*   **MAP 3.4: Processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness – and relevant technical standards and certifications – are defined, assessed, and documented.** This focuses on establishing, evaluating, and documenting the procedures that ensure human operators and practitioners are competent in using the AI system effectively, understand its performance and trustworthiness, and are aware of relevant technical standards and certifications.
*   **MAP 3.5: Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies from the GOVERN function.** This subcategory requires the clear definition, assessment, and documentation of procedures for human supervision of AI systems, ensuring these processes align with the broader governance policies established under the GOVERN function. Title: Applications: Scientific and Medical Research

LMMs are extending ways in which AI can support scientific and medical research. They can generate text to be used in scientific article, for submitting manuscripts or in writing peer review. They can be used to summarize texts including summaries for academic papers or can generate abstracts. LMMs can be used to analyse and summarize data to gain new insights in clinical and scientific research. They can be used to edit text, improving grammar, readability and conciseness of written documents such as articles and grant proposals. LMMs can be used to gain insights from data with which it was trained. One LMM trained on millions of academic articles is claimed to be able to analyse scientific research to answer questions, extract information or generate relevant text. However, concerns include lack of accountability, high-income country bias, hallucination and misinformation, and undermining of trust in peer review process. SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 11

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | MAP Function > Category 5
SECTION: MAP Function > Category 5 -- Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized.
TOPIC: This section outlines the subcategory within MAP 5, focusing on characterizing the likelihood and magnitude of both beneficial and harmful impacts of AI systems on individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society.
---
MAP 5 is dedicated to characterizing the impacts of AI systems on a broad spectrum of stakeholders, including individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society at large. This category ensures a holistic understanding of the AI system's potential effects beyond its immediate technical functionality. The subcategory under MAP 5 includes:

*   **MAP 5.1: Likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact (both potentially beneficial and harmful) based on expected use, past uses of AI systems in similar contexts, public incident reports, feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system, or other data are identified and documented.** This subcategory requires a systematic process for identifying and documenting the probability and severity (or positivity) of every potential impact. This assessment should draw upon various sources of information, including the AI system's intended use, historical data from similar AI deployments, publicly available incident reports, and crucial feedback gathered from external stakeholders who are not directly involved in the system's development or deployment. This comprehensive approach ensures that both positive and negative consequences are thoroughly considered and recorded. SOURCE: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence | Section IV.1
Title: POLICY AREA 1: ETHICAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT

Member States and relevant stakeholders should establish and maintain processes for conducting ethical impact assessments (EIAs) of AI systems before deployment, particularly for high-risk applications. EIAs should identify potential impacts on human rights, dignity, and the environment. These assessments should be ongoing and adaptive, with mechanisms for addressing identified risks. Documentation of EIAs should be maintained and made available to relevant authorities. Stakeholder consultation should be integral to the EIA process. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 05.7
Title: Societal Risk: Carbon and Water Footprint of LMMs

Another societal risk is carbon and water footprints of LMMs, which like other forms of AI require both significant energy and contribute to AI's growing water footprint. While LMMs and other forms of AI can provide important societal benefits, growing carbon footprint may become major contributor to climate change, and increasing water consumption can have further negative impact in water-stressed communities. Training large AI models requires enormous amounts of electricity, often generated from fossil fuels. Water is consumed both for cooling data centers and in electricity generation. Environmental sustainability must be factored into decisions about development and deployment of LMMs, particularly given urgent need to address climate change and water scarcity affecting many vulnerable populations globally.

SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.1.03
Title: Central Function: Risk Assessment and Monitoring

The government has established a central function within DSIT with multiple activities: (1) Risk assessment - recruited new multidisciplinary team to undertake cross-sectoral risk monitoring, bringing together expertise in risk, regulation, and AI with backgrounds in data science, engineering, economics, and law. This team will provide continuous examination of cross-cutting AI risks, including evaluating effectiveness of interventions by government and regulators. In 2024, targeted consultation on a cross-economy AI risk register will be launched to ensure it comprehensively captures range of risks. The register will provide single source of truth on AI risks for regulators, government departments, and external groups. It will support identifying risks that fall across or between regulator remits to identify gaps or where existing regulation is ineffective. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization
SECTION: Part 1: Foundational Information > 1.2 Challenges for AI Risk Management > 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization
TOPIC: This section explains the importance of prioritizing AI risks based on their potential impact, provides guidance on managing unacceptable risk levels, and discusses how prioritization may vary depending on AI system characteristics and interaction with humans.
---
In the practical application of AI risk management, attempting to eliminate all negative risk entirely can be counterproductive, as it is unrealistic to expect that all incidents and failures can be prevented. Unrealistic expectations regarding risk can lead organizations to allocate resources inefficiently, making risk triage impractical or wasting scarce resources. Cultivating a robust risk management culture within an organization helps in recognizing that not all AI risks are equivalent, thereby enabling the purposeful allocation of resources. Effective and actionable risk management efforts establish clear guidelines for assessing the trustworthiness of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources **should** be prioritized based on the assessed risk level and the potential impact of an AI system. The extent to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the AI deployer can also be a significant contributing factor to its risk profile.

When applying the AI RMF, risks that an organization determines to be highest for its AI systems within a given context of use demand the most urgent prioritization and the most thorough risk management process. In critical cases where an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk levels – such as situations where significant negative impacts are imminent, severe harms are actively occurring, or catastrophic risks are present – the development and deployment of that system **should** cease in a safe and controlled manner until the risks can be sufficiently managed and mitigated. Conversely, if an AI system's development, deployment, and use cases are found to be low-risk in a specific context, this may suggest a potentially lower initial prioritization for its risk management efforts.

Risk prioritization may also differ significantly between AI systems designed or deployed to directly interact with humans compared to those that do not. Higher initial prioritization may be warranted in settings where the AI system is trained on large datasets comprising sensitive or protected data, such as personally identifiable information, or where the outputs of the AI systems have a direct or indirect impact on human beings. In contrast, AI systems designed to interact solely with computational systems and trained on non-sensitive datasets (for example, data collected exclusively from the physical environment) may call for lower initial prioritization. Nevertheless, regularly assessing and prioritizing risk based on context remains crucial, as even non-human-facing AI systems can have significant downstream safety or social implications.

**Residual risk** – defined as the risk that remains after all risk treatment measures have been implemented – directly impacts end users or affected individuals and communities. Documenting these residual risks is essential, as it requires the system provider to fully consider the remaining risks of deploying the AI product and serves to inform end users about the potential negative impacts of interacting with the system. This transparency is vital for fostering trust and enabling informed decision-making by users. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | Executive Summary
SECTION: Executive Summary
TOPIC: This chunk introduces the dual nature of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, highlighting their transformative potential alongside the diverse risks they pose, and provides a foundational definition of an AI system.
---
Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies possess immense potential to profoundly transform society and individuals' lives across various sectors, including commerce, health, transportation, cybersecurity, and environmental management. These technologies are capable of driving inclusive economic growth and fostering scientific advancements that contribute to improving global conditions. However, alongside these significant benefits, AI technologies also introduce a range of risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, communities, society, the environment, and the planet. These AI-related risks can manifest in diverse ways, characterized by their duration (long- or short-term), likelihood (high- or low-probability), scope (systemic or localized), and severity of impact (high- or low-impact).
Within the context of the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), an "AI system" is specifically defined as an engineered or machine-based system. The core capability of such a system is to generate outputs, such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions, for a given set of objectives. These outputs are designed to influence either real or virtual environments. Furthermore, AI systems are developed to operate with varying degrees of autonomy, meaning their ability to function independently can differ significantly based on their design and purpose. This definition is adapted from established international sources, including the OECD Recommendation on AI (2019) and ISO/IEC 22989:2022, providing a consistent understanding for risk management purposes.

SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 21
TITLE: Human oversight

High-risk AI systems shall be designed and operated in a way that enables human oversight. Users shall be able to understand the outputs of the AI system and to intervene or interrupt the system's operation when necessary. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
SECTION: Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
TOPIC: This section details how the GOVERN and MAP functions of the AI RMF provide mechanisms to address human-AI interaction challenges, emphasizing the importance of diverse teams and outlining areas for ongoing research.
---
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) provides specific opportunities within its functions to address the complexities of human-AI interaction. The **GOVERN** function, for instance, offers organizations the means to clarify and define the roles and responsibilities for humans within Human-AI team configurations and for those overseeing AI system performance. Furthermore, the GOVERN function establishes mechanisms for organizations to make their decision-making processes more explicit, which helps to counter systemic biases that can arise during AI development and deployment.

Similarly, the **MAP** function suggests opportunities to define and document processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness concepts. It also encourages the definition of relevant technical standards and certifications. Implementing categories and subcategories within the MAP function can significantly help organizations improve their internal competency for analyzing context, identifying procedural and system limitations, exploring and examining the real-world impacts of AI-based systems, and evaluating decision-making processes throughout the entire AI lifecycle.

Both the GOVERN and MAP functions underscore the importance of interdisciplinarity and demographically diverse teams. They also highlight the value of utilizing feedback from potentially impacted individuals and communities. AI actors, particularly those performing human factors tasks and activities as called out in the AI RMF, can provide crucial assistance to technical teams. They help anchor design and development practices to user intentions and representatives of the broader AI community and societal values. These actors further aid in incorporating context-specific norms and values into system design and evaluating end-user experiences in conjunction with AI systems.

AI risk management approaches for human-AI configurations will be continuously augmented by ongoing research and evaluation. For example, the degree to which humans are empowered and incentivized to challenge AI system output requires further studies. Collecting and analyzing data about the frequency and rationale with which humans overrule AI system output in deployed systems may prove highly useful for future improvements. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 09.3
Title: Deployment Phase: Healthcare Worker Training and Education

Health-worker training is critical to ensure that when they use LMM professionally, their duties do not unknowingly violate laws, especially those related to protection of health data and information. Medical providers who introduce protected health information into LMM chatbot may be violating data protection laws. As popular LMMs become trusted by health-care workers, they may disclose more patient data than they realize. Ministries of health and universities should train health-care professionals and clinicians to understand how LMMs make decisions and limits of understanding how such decisions are made, to identify and understand concerns about appropriate use, in methods to avoid automation bias, to engage with and educate patients who may be or are considering use of LMMs, and on cybersecurity risks associated with use of LMMs.

SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 5.2
Title: Human Alternatives: Fallback and Escalation Process

You should have access to timely human consideration and remedy by a fallback and escalation process if an automated system fails, it produces an error, or you would like to appeal or contest its impacts on you. Human consideration and fallback should be accessible, equitable, effective, maintained, accompanied by appropriate operator training, and should not impose an unreasonable burden on the public. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | MANAGE 4
SECTION: MANAGE Function > Category 4
TOPIC: How organizations should document and regularly monitor risk treatment, response, and communication plans for identified and measured AI risks, including post-deployment monitoring and continual improvement activities.
---
**MANAGE 4: Risk treatments, including response and recovery, and communication plans for the identified and measured AI risks are documented and monitored regularly.** This category focuses on the operational aspects of risk management post-deployment, ensuring that organizations have robust plans for monitoring, incident response, recovery, and continuous improvement. It emphasizes the importance of communication with all relevant AI actors, including affected communities, regarding incidents and system updates, fostering transparency and trust.

Specifically, organizations should address the following subcategories:

- **MANAGE 4.1:** Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.
- **MANAGE 4.2:** Measurable activities for continual improvements are integrated into AI system updates and include regular engagement with interested parties, including relevant AI actors.
- **MANAGE 4.3:** Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities. Processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors are followed and documented. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education.

gap_description.what_is_missing:
Five compounding deficiencies collectively leave the incident response lifecycle incomplete for a PG-level general utility/productivity system serving students:

1. **No student-facing reporting or appeal mechanism** — the process relies exclusively on staff detection, meaning student-experienced harms (e.g., harmful AI outputs received directly) have no accessible, documented channel for self-reporting or appeal, contrary to Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights §5.2.

2. **No defined recovery or post-incident review timeline** — beyond an initial pause, there is no documented schedule or owner for recovery actions, root-cause analysis, or change management steps (MANAGE 4.1).

3. **No stakeholder communication plan** — there is no documented protocol specifying who is notified, through what channel, within what timeframe, and with what content when an incident affects students or the broader community (MANAGE 4.3).

4. **No continual improvement metrics or activities tied to incident trends** — there are no measurable KPIs, review cadences, or feedback loops that use incident data to drive systemic improvement (MANAGE 4.2).

5. **No incident logging or tracking system** — resolved and ongoing incidents are not recorded in any auditable system, making it impossible to demonstrate accountability, pattern detection, or compliance evidence to a Certifier (MANAGE 4.3).
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap in sequence before the Certifier phase:

**Gap 1 — Student reporting & appeal channel:**
- Design and publish a clearly accessible student-facing mechanism (e.g., an in-system "Report a Concern" button, a dedicated email alias, or a web form) for reporting harmful AI outputs.
- Document the appeal pathway, including who receives reports, acknowledgement SLAs, and how outcomes are communicated back to the student.
- Reference Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights §5.2 explicitly in the policy to demonstrate alignment.

**Gap 2 — Recovery & post-incident review timeline:**
- Amend the incident response policy to define explicit timeframes: e.g., initial triage within 2 hours, recovery action within 24 hours, root-cause analysis (RCA) completed within 5 business days, change management sign-off within 10 business days.

SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.05
Title: Highly Capable AI: Emerging Safety Processes Framework

Ahead of AI Safety Summit, UK government outlined set of emerging safety processes to provide information to companies on ensuring and maintaining safety of AI technologies. Document covers nine emerging processes: (1) Responsible Capability Scaling - framework for managing risk as organizations scale capability of frontier AI systems; (2) Model Evaluations and Red Teaming - methods to assess risks AI systems pose; (3) Model Reporting and Information Sharing - practices that increase government visibility of frontier AI development and deployment; (4) Security Controls including Securing Model Weights - measures such as cyber security that underpin AI system security; (5) Reporting Structure for Vulnerabilities - process to enable outsiders to identify safety and security issues; (6) Identifiers of AI-generated Material - tools to mitigate creation and distribution of deceptive AI-generated content; (7) Prioritising Research on Risks Posed by AI; (8) Preventing and Monitoring Model Misuse; (9) Data Input Controls and Audits - measures to identify and manage training data that is likely to increase dangerous capabilities. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 15.1
Title: Regulatory Risks: Compliance with Legal and Data Protection Requirements

Broader regulatory and systemic risks could emerge with use of LMMs. One concern being examined by several data protection authorities is whether LMMs comply with existing legal or regulatory regimes including international human rights obligations and national data protection regulations. Algorithms might not comply with such laws because of way in which data are collected to train LMMs, management and processing of data that have been collected or put into LMMs by end users, transparency and accountability of entities that develop LMMs, and possibility that LMMs hallucinate. LMMs could also be non-compliant with consumer protection laws. Leading medical and scientific journals have already responded to emergence of LMMs. One academic publisher set two rules: LMM will not be accepted as credited author on research paper, and researchers using LMMs should document their use in methods section and acknowledgements. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.1.03
Title: Central Function: Risk Assessment and Monitoring

The government has established a central function within DSIT with multiple activities: (1) Risk assessment - recruited new multidisciplinary team to undertake cross-sectoral risk monitoring, bringing together expertise in risk, regulation, and AI with backgrounds in data science, engineering, economics, and law. This team will provide continuous examination of cross-cutting AI risks, including evaluating effectiveness of interventions by government and regulators. In 2024, targeted consultation on a cross-economy AI risk register will be launched to ensure it comprehensively captures range of risks. The register will provide single source of truth on AI risks for regulators, government departments, and external groups. It will support identifying risks that fall across or between regulator remits to identify gaps or where existing regulation is ineffective.

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | AI Actors and their Tasks
SECTION: AI Actors and their Tasks: Specific Roles
TOPIC: The NIST AI RMF defines various AI actor roles, including Human Factors, Domain Experts, AI Impact Assessors, Procurement, and Governance and Oversight, outlining their distinct responsibilities in managing AI risks.
---
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) identifies several key AI actor roles, each with specific tasks and responsibilities crucial for effective AI risk management across the AI lifecycle:

*   **Human Factors** tasks and activities are integrated throughout all dimensions of the AI lifecycle. These include implementing human-centered design practices and methodologies, actively involving end users and other interested parties, incorporating context-specific norms and values into system design, evaluating and adapting end-user experiences, and broadly integrating human dynamics into all phases. Human factors professionals contribute multidisciplinary skills to understand context of use, inform diversity, engage in consultative processes, design user experience, perform human-centered evaluation, and inform impact assessments.

*   **Domain Expert** tasks involve input from multidisciplinary practitioners or scholars who provide specialized knowledge or expertise within a specific industry sector, economic sector, context, or application area where an AI system is being used. These AI actors offer essential guidance for AI system design and development and help interpret outputs to support the work of TEVV and AI impact assessment teams.

*   **AI Impact Assessment** tasks include evaluating requirements for AI system accountability, combating harmful bias, examining the broader impacts of AI systems, and assessing product safety, liability, and security, among other critical areas. AI actors in this role, such as impact assessors and evaluators, provide technical, human factor, socio-cultural, and legal expertise.

*   **Procurement** tasks are conducted by AI actors with financial, legal, or policy management authority. Their role involves the acquisition of AI models, products, or services from third-party developers, vendors, or contractors, ensuring that procured AI aligns with organizational risk management strategies.

*   **Governance and Oversight** tasks are assumed by AI actors with management, fiduciary, and legal authority and responsibility for the organization where an AI system is designed, developed, and/or deployed. Key actors include organizational management, senior leadership, and the Board of Directors, who are concerned with the overall impact and sustainability of the organization. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | Appendix A
SECTION: Appendix A: Descriptions of AI Actor Tasks
TOPIC: A comprehensive description of the tasks performed by various AI actors across the AI lifecycle, including design, development, deployment, operation, monitoring, and test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV).
---
Appendix A provides descriptions of key AI Actor tasks across the AI lifecycle, as referenced in Figures 2 and 3 of the NIST AI RMF. These descriptions clarify the responsibilities and activities of various stakeholders involved in the design, development, deployment, and ongoing operation of AI systems. Understanding these roles is crucial for effective AI risk management, as it helps in assigning accountability and ensuring comprehensive oversight throughout the system's lifespan.

The primary AI Actor tasks include:

- **AI Design** tasks are performed during the Application Context and Data and Input phases of the AI lifecycle. AI Design actors create the concept and objectives of AI systems and are responsible for the planning, design, and data collection and processing tasks of the AI system so that the AI system is lawful and fit-for-purpose. Tasks include articulating and documenting the system’s concept and objectives, underlying assumptions, context, and requirements; gathering and cleaning data; and documenting the metadata and characteristics of the dataset. AI actors in this category include data scientists, domain experts, socio-cultural analysts, experts in the field of diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility, members of impacted communities, human factors experts (e.g., UX/UI design), governance experts, data engineers, data providers, system funders, product managers, third-party entities, evaluators, and legal and privacy governance.

- **AI Development** tasks are performed during the AI Model phase of the lifecycle. AI Development actors provide the initial infrastructure of AI systems and are responsible for model building and interpretation tasks, which involve the creation, selection, calibration, training, and/or testing of models or algorithms. AI actors in this category include machine learning experts, data scientists, developers, third-party entities, legal and privacy governance experts, and experts in the socio-cultural and contextual factors associated with the deployment setting.

- **AI Deployment** tasks are performed during the Task and Output phase of the lifecycle. AI Deployment actors are responsible for contextual decisions relating to how the AI system is used to assure deployment of the system into production. Related tasks include piloting the system, checking compatibility with legacy systems, ensuring regulatory compliance, managing organizational change, and evaluating user experience. AI actors in this category include system integrators, software developers, end users, operators and practitioners, evaluators, and domain experts with expertise in human factors, socio-cultural analysis, and governance.

- **Operation and Monitoring** tasks are performed in the Application Context/Operate and Monitor phase of the lifecycle. These tasks are carried out by AI actors who are responsible for operating the AI system and working with others to regularly assess system output and impacts. AI actors in this category include system operators, domain experts, AI designers, users who interpret or incorporate the output of AI systems, product developers, evaluators and auditors, compliance experts, organizational management, and members of the research community.

- **Test, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation (TEVV)** tasks are performed throughout the AI lifecycle. They are carried out by AI actors who examine the AI system or its components, or detect and remediate problems. This continuous process is vital for ensuring the trustworthiness and reliability of AI systems at every stage, from initial design to post-deployment monitoring. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.04
Title: Highly Capable AI: AI Safety Institute Core Functions

The AI Safety Institute will perform three core functions: (1) Develop and conduct evaluations on advanced AI systems, aiming to characterise safety-relevant capabilities, understand safety and security of systems, and assess their societal impacts; (2) Drive foundational AI safety research to support short and long-term AI governance, ensuring UK's iterative regulatory framework for AI is informed by latest expertise and laying foundation for technically grounded international governance of advanced AI, with projects ranging from rapid development of tools to inform governance to exploratory AI safety research which may be underexplored by industry; (3) Facilitate information exchange by establishing - on voluntary basis and subject to existing privacy and data regulation - clear information-sharing channels between Institute and other national and international actors such as policymakers, international partners, private companies, academia, civil society, and broader public. The AI Safety Institute is not a regulator; its role is to develop technical expertise to understand capabilities and risks of AI systems.

SECTION: Appendix C: AI Risk Management and Human-AI Interaction
TOPIC: This section details how the GOVERN and MAP functions of the AI RMF provide mechanisms to address human-AI interaction challenges, emphasizing the importance of diverse teams and outlining areas for ongoing research.
---
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) provides specific opportunities within its functions to address the complexities of human-AI interaction. The **GOVERN** function, for instance, offers organizations the means to clarify and define the roles and responsibilities for humans within Human-AI team configurations and for those overseeing AI system performance. Furthermore, the GOVERN function establishes mechanisms for organizations to make their decision-making processes more explicit, which helps to counter systemic biases that can arise during AI development and deployment.

Similarly, the **MAP** function suggests opportunities to define and document processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness concepts. It also encourages the definition of relevant technical standards and certifications. Implementing categories and subcategories within the MAP function can significantly help organizations improve their internal competency for analyzing context, identifying procedural and system limitations, exploring and examining the real-world impacts of AI-based systems, and evaluating decision-making processes throughout the entire AI lifecycle.

Both the GOVERN and MAP functions underscore the importance of interdisciplinarity and demographically diverse teams. They also highlight the value of utilizing feedback from potentially impacted individuals and communities. AI actors, particularly those performing human factors tasks and activities as called out in the AI RMF, can provide crucial assistance to technical teams. They help anchor design and development practices to user intentions and representatives of the broader AI community and societal values. These actors further aid in incorporating context-specific norms and values into system design and evaluating end-user experiences in conjunction with AI systems.

AI risk management approaches for human-AI configurations will be continuously augmented by ongoing research and evaluation. For example, the degree to which humans are empowered and incentivized to challenge AI system output requires further studies. Collecting and analyzing data about the frequency and rationale with which humans overrule AI system output in deployed systems may prove highly useful for future improvements.

Five distinct deficiencies collectively undermine the control's readiness across all three required intervention dimensions (override, review, escalation):

1. **No formal escalation pathway beyond halt**: There is no structured, documented process enabling staff to escalate concerns about AI output quality or errors to a higher authority or designated review body — the current mechanism stops at halt/override with no upward referral chain.

SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 14.1
Title: Applications: Clerical Functions and Administrative Tasks

LMMs are being used to assist health professionals in clerical, administrative and financial aspects of practising medicine. Medicine exposes physicians and other health-care professionals to ever-growing paperwork for numerous obligations for recording patient information and data in electronic health records, billing and other administrative tasks. Documentation constituted one fourth to one half of doctor's time and one fifth of nurse's time. LMMs have been singled out as means of returning time to health-care professionals to reduce burn-out and allocate more time to providing care. Examples of uses include better communication to assist in translation, to fill in missing information in electronic health records, and to draft clinical notes after each patient visit. However, serious errors could arise due to inaccuracies, mistakes or hallucinations. LMMs can be inconsistent with slight changes to prompt generating completely different electronic health record. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.2
Title: Applications: Scientific and Medical Research

LMMs are extending ways in which AI can support scientific and medical research. They can generate text to be used in scientific article, for submitting manuscripts or in writing peer review. They can be used to summarize texts including summaries for academic papers or can generate abstracts. LMMs can be used to analyse and summarize data to gain new insights in clinical and scientific research. They can be used to edit text, improving grammar, readability and conciseness of written documents such as articles and grant proposals. LMMs can be used to gain insights from data with which it was trained. One LMM trained on millions of academic articles is claimed to be able to analyse scientific research to answer questions, extract information or generate relevant text. However, concerns include lack of accountability, high-income country bias, hallucination and misinformation, and undermining of trust in peer review process. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education.

SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 3.6
Title: Data Privacy: Use-Specific Consent

Consent practices should not allow for abusive surveillance practices. Where data collectors or automated systems seek consent, they should seek it for specific, narrow use contexts, for specific time durations, and for use by specific entities. Consent should not extend if any of these conditions change; consent should be re-acquired before using data if the use case changes, a time limit elapses, or data is transferred to another entity. When seeking consent from users short, plain language consent requests should be used so that users understand for what use contexts, time span, and entities they are providing data and metadata consent. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 07.3
Title: Development Phase: Data Protection Laws and Informed Consent

WHO supports application and enforcement of standards including data protection rules that govern how data have and will be used to train LMMs. Data protection laws are usually based on rights-based approaches and include standards for regulation of data-processing that both protect rights of individuals and establish obligations for public and private data controllers and processers. As data protection laws have been adopted in over 150 countries, they provide solid foundation for development of all AI technologies including LMMs. One requirement of data protection that should be enforced is that data are obtained and processed lawfully. This will often require provision of meaningful informed consent by data subject for use of their data for stated purpose. Any further processing should have its own legal basis. Pursuit of ever-larger LMMs requiring increasingly larger data sets may lead developers to ignore legal requirements. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 09.3
Title: Deployment Phase: Healthcare Worker Training and Education

Health-worker training is critical to ensure that when they use LMM professionally, their duties do not unknowingly violate laws, especially those related to protection of health data and information. Medical providers who introduce protected health information into LMM chatbot may be violating data protection laws. As popular LMMs become trusted by health-care workers, they may disclose more patient data than they realize. Ministries of health and universities should train health-care professionals and clinicians to understand how LMMs make decisions and limits of understanding how such decisions are made, to identify and understand concerns about appropriate use, in methods to avoid automation bias, to engage with and educate patients who may be or are considering use of LMMs, and on cybersecurity risks associated with use of LMMs.
