SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 1.4a
Title- PRINCIPLE 1.4a: ROBUSTNESS, SECURITY AND SAFETY - CORE REQUIREMENTS

AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks. This requires comprehensive testing, validation, and ongoing monitoring to ensure AI systems behave as intended and remain safe across a range of operating conditions and potential misuse scenarios. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 3.6 Privacy-Enhanced
SECTION: 3.6 Privacy-Enhanced
TOPIC: The definition of privacy in AI, the values that should guide AI system design, and how privacy-enhancing technologies and data minimization methods can mitigate privacy-related risks and tradeoffs.
---
Privacy refers generally to the norms and practices that help to safeguard human autonomy, identity, and dignity. These norms and practices typically address freedom from intrusion, limiting observation, or individuals’ agency to consent to disclosure or control of facets of their identities (e.g., body, data, reputation). (See The NIST Privacy Framework: A Tool for Improving Privacy through Enterprise Risk Management.)

Privacy values such as anonymity, confidentiality, and control generally should guide choices for AI system design, development, and deployment. Privacy-related risks may influence security, bias, and transparency and come with tradeoffs with these other characteristics. Like safety and security, specific technical features of an AI system may promote or reduce privacy. AI systems can also present new risks to privacy by allowing inference to identify individuals or previously private information about individuals.

Privacy-enhancing technologies (“PETs”) for AI, as well as data minimizing methods such as de-identification and aggregation for certain model outputs, can support design for privacy-enhanced AI systems. Under certain conditions such as data sparsity, privacy-enhancing techniques can result in a loss in accuracy, affecting decisions about fairness and other values in certain domains.

1. ACCESS LOGGING & AUDIT TRAILS — Enable and configure access logging (e.g., authentication logs, privilege-use logs) for all seven permitted accounts. JOINER/MOVER/LEAVER (JML) PROCESS — Draft and formally approve a written SOP covering the end-to-end process for granting, modifying, and revoking access upon staff onboarding, role reassignment, and departure. Provide at least one completed example record (e.g., a leaver ticket or access-change log entry) as operational proof.

Produce a policy or SOP defining the review cadence, the responsible reviewer(s), the acceptance criteria, and the remediation process for inappropriate accounts. Provide evidence of at least one completed review cycle (e.g., a signed access review register or report).

4. DATA MINIMISATION & PRIVACY-ENHANCING MEASURES — Document the data minimisation approach applied to data handled within the system (e.g., collection limitation, pseudonymisation, masking, retention limits, purpose binding). Map these measures explicitly to NIST AI RMF privacy subcategories and any applicable privacy regulations. Include this as a dedicated section within the control document or as a referenced privacy impact artefact.

SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 1.7
Title: Safe Systems: Data Quality and Relevance

Data used as part of any automated system's creation, evaluation, or deployment should be relevant, of high quality, and tailored to the task at hand. Relevancy should be established based on research-backed demonstration of the causal influence of the data to the specific use case. High quality and tailored data should be representative of the task at hand and errors from data entry or other sources should be measured and limited. Any data used as the target of a prediction process should receive particular attention to the quality and validity of the predicted outcome or label. Justification should be documented for each data attribute and source. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 2.1b
Title- RECOMMENDATION 2.1b: OPEN-SOURCE TOOLS AND DATASETS

Governments should also consider public investment and encourage private investment in open-source tools and open datasets that are representative and respect privacy and data protection to support an environment for AI research and development that is free of harmful bias and to improve interoperability and use of standards. Open resources promote transparency, enable independent verification, and democratize access to AI development capabilities while ensuring quality and representativeness of training data.

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | MAP Function > Category 1
SECTION: MAP Function > Category 1 -- Context is established and understood.
TOPIC: This section outlines the subcategories within MAP 1, focusing on establishing and thoroughly understanding the context in which an AI system will operate, including its purposes, impacts, and organizational goals.
---
MAP 1 is a foundational category within the MAP function, emphasizing that the context for an AI system must be thoroughly established and understood. This involves a comprehensive examination of various factors that define the operational environment and potential implications of the AI system. The subcategories under MAP 1 include:

*   **MAP 1.1: Intended purposes, potentially beneficial uses, context-specific laws, norms and expectations, and prospective settings in which the AI system will be deployed are understood and documented.** This subcategory requires a detailed understanding and documentation of the AI system's explicit goals, potential positive applications, relevant legal and social frameworks, and the specific environments where it will be used. Considerations include the types of users and their expectations, potential positive and negative impacts on individuals, communities, organizations, society, and the planet, assumptions and limitations regarding purposes, uses, and risks across the AI lifecycle, and related Testing, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation (TEVV) and system metrics.
*   **MAP 1.2: Interdisciplinary AI actors, competencies, skills, and capacities for establishing context reflect demographic diversity and broad domain and user experience expertise, and their participation is documented. Opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration are prioritized.** This emphasizes the importance of involving a diverse group of experts with varied backgrounds and experiences in the process of defining the AI system's context, ensuring that their contributions are recorded and that collaborative efforts are actively encouraged.
*   **MAP 1.3: The organization’s mission and relevant goals for AI technology are understood and documented.** This subcategory ensures that the AI system's development and deployment align with the organization's overarching strategic objectives and mission.
*   **MAP 1.4: The business value or context of business use has been clearly defined or – in the case of assessing existing AI systems – re-evaluated.** This focuses on articulating the clear economic or operational justification for the AI system, or reassessing it for existing systems.
*   **MAP 1.5: Organizational risk tolerances are determined and documented.** This requires organizations to explicitly define and record their acceptable levels of risk, which will guide subsequent risk management activities.
*   **MAP 1.6: System requirements (e.g., “the system shall respect the privacy of its users”) are elicited from and understood by relevant AI actors. Design decisions take socio-technical implications into account to address AI risks.** This subcategory ensures that technical specifications are derived from stakeholder needs and that design choices consider both technical and social factors to mitigate AI-related risks effectively. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | GOVERN Function > Category 5
SECTION: GOVERN Function > Category 5 -- Processes are in place for robust engagement with relevant AI actors.
TOPIC: This section outlines the subcategories within GOVERN 5, focusing on establishing processes for robust engagement with external AI actors to collect and integrate feedback on potential individual and societal impacts of AI systems.
---
GOVERN 5 emphasizes the establishment of processes for robust engagement with relevant AI actors external to the organization. This category recognizes the importance of external perspectives in comprehensively understanding and managing the broader impacts and risks of AI systems. The subcategories under GOVERN 5 include:

*   **GOVERN 5.1: Organizational policies and practices are in place to collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system regarding the potential individual and societal impacts related to AI risks.** This subcategory requires organizations to implement formal mechanisms for gathering, evaluating, and incorporating feedback from a wide range of external stakeholders, including affected individuals and communities, to inform their understanding of AI risks and impacts.
*   **GOVERN 5.2: Mechanisms are established to enable the team that developed or deployed AI systems to regularly incorporate adjudicated feedback from relevant AI actors into system design and implementation.** This focuses on creating structured pathways for development and deployment teams to systematically review and integrate validated external feedback into the ongoing design, refinement, and implementation of AI systems, ensuring continuous improvement based on real-world insights. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 2. Audience
SECTION: Part 1: Foundational Information > 2. Audience
TOPIC: This section identifies the broad audience of AI actors involved in AI risk management across the AI lifecycle, emphasizing the importance of diverse perspectives and introducing the key socio-technical dimensions of AI systems.
---
Identifying and effectively managing AI risks and their potential impacts – encompassing both positive and negative outcomes – necessitates a broad spectrum of perspectives and active participation from various actors throughout the entire AI lifecycle. Ideally, these AI actors **should** represent a diversity of experience, expertise, and backgrounds, forming demographically and disciplinarily diverse teams. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is specifically intended for use by all AI actors across the AI lifecycle and its various dimensions.

The OECD has developed a foundational framework for classifying AI lifecycle activities, structured around five key socio-technical dimensions. Each of these dimensions possesses properties highly relevant for AI policy, governance, and crucially, risk management. NIST has slightly modified this OECD framework for the purposes of the AI RMF, primarily to highlight the critical importance of Test, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation (TEVV) processes throughout an AI lifecycle, and to generalize the operational context of an AI system.

The core AI dimensions displayed in Figure 2 (Lifecycle and Key Dimensions of an AI System, which illustrates the Application Context, Data and Input, AI Model, and Task and Output) are central to understanding where AI risks manifest. AI actors involved in these dimensions, who perform or manage the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems, and who drive AI risk management efforts, constitute the **primary** audience for the AI RMF. Representative AI actors across these lifecycle dimensions are further detailed in Figure 3 and described comprehensively in Appendix A of the document. Within the AI RMF, the expectation is that all AI actors collaborate to manage risks and collectively achieve the overarching goals of trustworthy and responsible AI.

AI actors with specific TEVV expertise are integrated throughout the AI lifecycle and are particularly likely to benefit from the Framework. Performed regularly and systematically, TEVV tasks can provide invaluable insights relative to technical, societal, legal, and ethical standards or norms. These processes are instrumental in assisting with anticipating potential impacts and in assessing and tracking emergent risks. As a regular and continuous process within an AI lifecycle, TEVV allows for both mid-course remediation of issues and effective post-hoc risk management, ensuring that systems remain aligned with trustworthiness objectives as they evolve.

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization
SECTION: Part 1: Foundational Information > 1.2 Challenges for AI Risk Management > 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization
TOPIC: This section explains the importance of prioritizing AI risks based on their potential impact, provides guidance on managing unacceptable risk levels, and discusses how prioritization may vary depending on AI system characteristics and interaction with humans.
---
In the practical application of AI risk management, attempting to eliminate all negative risk entirely can be counterproductive, as it is unrealistic to expect that all incidents and failures can be prevented. Unrealistic expectations regarding risk can lead organizations to allocate resources inefficiently, making risk triage impractical or wasting scarce resources. Cultivating a robust risk management culture within an organization helps in recognizing that not all AI risks are equivalent, thereby enabling the purposeful allocation of resources. Effective and actionable risk management efforts establish clear guidelines for assessing the trustworthiness of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources **should** be prioritized based on the assessed risk level and the potential impact of an AI system. The extent to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the AI deployer can also be a significant contributing factor to its risk profile.

When applying the AI RMF, risks that an organization determines to be highest for its AI systems within a given context of use demand the most urgent prioritization and the most thorough risk management process. In critical cases where an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk levels – such as situations where significant negative impacts are imminent, severe harms are actively occurring, or catastrophic risks are present – the development and deployment of that system **should** cease in a safe and controlled manner until the risks can be sufficiently managed and mitigated. Conversely, if an AI system's development, deployment, and use cases are found to be low-risk in a specific context, this may suggest a potentially lower initial prioritization for its risk management efforts.

Risk prioritization may also differ significantly between AI systems designed or deployed to directly interact with humans compared to those that do not. Higher initial prioritization may be warranted in settings where the AI system is trained on large datasets comprising sensitive or protected data, such as personally identifiable information, or where the outputs of the AI systems have a direct or indirect impact on human beings. In contrast, AI systems designed to interact solely with computational systems and trained on non-sensitive datasets (for example, data collected exclusively from the physical environment) may call for lower initial prioritization. Nevertheless, regularly assessing and prioritizing risk based on context remains crucial, as even non-human-facing AI systems can have significant downstream safety or social implications.

**Residual risk** – defined as the risk that remains after all risk treatment measures have been implemented – directly impacts end users or affected individuals and communities. Documenting these residual risks is essential, as it requires the system provider to fully consider the remaining risks of deploying the AI product and serves to inform end users about the potential negative impacts of interacting with the system. This transparency is vital for fostering trust and enabling informed decision-making by users. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.06
Title: Highly Capable AI: Case for Targeted Mandatory Interventions

Context-based approach may miss significant risks posed by highly capable general-purpose systems and leave developers of those systems unaccountable. Whilst voluntary measures are useful tool to address risks today, all jurisdictions will in time want to place targeted mandatory interventions on design, development, and deployment of such systems to ensure risks are adequately addressed. In line with proportionate approach, any future regulation would be targeted at small number of developers of most powerful general-purpose systems. This would be done by establishing dynamic thresholds that can quickly respond to advances in AI development. Preliminary analysis indicates initial thresholds could be based on forecasts of capabilities using combination of two proxies: compute (i.e. amount of compute used to train model) and capability benchmarking (assessing capabilities in certain risk areas to identify where high capabilities result in high risk). At least for time being, combination of these proxies can predict AI capabilities reasonably well, though there might need to be range of thresholds. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | MANAGE 1
SECTION: MANAGE Function > Category 1
TOPIC: How organizations should prioritize, respond to, and manage AI risks based on assessments from the MAP and MEASURE functions, including making deployment determinations and documenting residual risks.
---
**MANAGE 1: AI risks based on assessments and other analytical output from the MAP and MEASURE functions are prioritized, responded to, and managed.** This category focuses on making critical decisions about AI system deployment, prioritizing identified risks, developing appropriate responses, and documenting residual risks. It ensures that insights from the **MAP** and **MEASURE** functions are translated into actionable risk management strategies, providing a structured approach to addressing potential negative impacts and ensuring responsible AI system lifecycle management.

Specifically, organizations should address the following subcategories:

- **MANAGE 1.1:** A determination is made as to whether the AI system achieves its intended purposes and stated objectives and whether its development or deployment should proceed.
- **MANAGE 1.2:** Treatment of documented AI risks is prioritized based on impact, likelihood, and available resources or methods.
- **MANAGE 1.3:** Responses to the AI risks deemed high priority, as identified by the **MAP** function, are developed, planned, and documented. Risk response options can include mitigating, transferring, avoiding, or accepting.
- **MANAGE 1.4:** Negative residual risks (defined as the sum of all unmitigated risks) to both downstream acquirers of AI systems and end users are documented.

SOURCE: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence | Section IV.1
Title: POLICY AREA 1: ETHICAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT

Member States and relevant stakeholders should establish and maintain processes for conducting ethical impact assessments (EIAs) of AI systems before deployment, particularly for high-risk applications. EIAs should identify potential impacts on human rights, dignity, and the environment. These assessments should be ongoing and adaptive, with mechanisms for addressing identified risks. Documentation of EIAs should be maintained and made available to relevant authorities. Stakeholder consultation should be integral to the EIA process. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.2
Title: Applications: Scientific and Medical Research

LMMs are extending ways in which AI can support scientific and medical research. They can generate text to be used in scientific article, for submitting manuscripts or in writing peer review. They can be used to summarize texts including summaries for academic papers or can generate abstracts. LMMs can be used to analyse and summarize data to gain new insights in clinical and scientific research. They can be used to edit text, improving grammar, readability and conciseness of written documents such as articles and grant proposals. LMMs can be used to gain insights from data with which it was trained. One LMM trained on millions of academic articles is claimed to be able to analyse scientific research to answer questions, extract information or generate relevant text. However, concerns include lack of accountability, high-income country bias, hallucination and misinformation, and undermining of trust in peer review process. SOURCE: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence | Section V
Title: MONITORING AND EVALUATION

Member States should transparently and systematically monitor and evaluate AI ethics policies using quantitative and qualitative methods adapted to national contexts. UNESCO will support this through ethical impact assessment methodologies, readiness assessments, policy effectiveness evaluations, and evidence-based research and data sharing. Monitoring processes should be inclusive, ensuring participation of diverse and vulnerable groups, and strengthen transparency and accountability. Continuous, risk-proportionate evaluation should be based on internationally agreed frameworks, appropriate indicators, and lawful data practices, supported by mechanisms such as ethics commissions, observatories, regulatory sandboxes, and experience-sharing platforms.

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization
SECTION: Part 1: Foundational Information > 1.2 Challenges for AI Risk Management > 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization
TOPIC: This section explains the importance of prioritizing AI risks based on their potential impact, provides guidance on managing unacceptable risk levels, and discusses how prioritization may vary depending on AI system characteristics and interaction with humans.
---
In the practical application of AI risk management, attempting to eliminate all negative risk entirely can be counterproductive, as it is unrealistic to expect that all incidents and failures can be prevented. Unrealistic expectations regarding risk can lead organizations to allocate resources inefficiently, making risk triage impractical or wasting scarce resources. Cultivating a robust risk management culture within an organization helps in recognizing that not all AI risks are equivalent, thereby enabling the purposeful allocation of resources. Effective and actionable risk management efforts establish clear guidelines for assessing the trustworthiness of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources **should** be prioritized based on the assessed risk level and the potential impact of an AI system. The extent to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the AI deployer can also be a significant contributing factor to its risk profile.

When applying the AI RMF, risks that an organization determines to be highest for its AI systems within a given context of use demand the most urgent prioritization and the most thorough risk management process. In critical cases where an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk levels – such as situations where significant negative impacts are imminent, severe harms are actively occurring, or catastrophic risks are present – the development and deployment of that system **should** cease in a safe and controlled manner until the risks can be sufficiently managed and mitigated. Conversely, if an AI system's development, deployment, and use cases are found to be low-risk in a specific context, this may suggest a potentially lower initial prioritization for its risk management efforts.

Risk prioritization may also differ significantly between AI systems designed or deployed to directly interact with humans compared to those that do not. Higher initial prioritization may be warranted in settings where the AI system is trained on large datasets comprising sensitive or protected data, such as personally identifiable information, or where the outputs of the AI systems have a direct or indirect impact on human beings. In contrast, AI systems designed to interact solely with computational systems and trained on non-sensitive datasets (for example, data collected exclusively from the physical environment) may call for lower initial prioritization. Nevertheless, regularly assessing and prioritizing risk based on context remains crucial, as even non-human-facing AI systems can have significant downstream safety or social implications.

**Residual risk** – defined as the risk that remains after all risk treatment measures have been implemented – directly impacts end users or affected individuals and communities. Documenting these residual risks is essential, as it requires the system provider to fully consider the remaining risks of deploying the AI product and serves to inform end users about the potential negative impacts of interacting with the system. This transparency is vital for fostering trust and enabling informed decision-making by users. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.02
Title: Highly Capable AI: Life Cycle Accountability Gaps

Many of UK's current legal frameworks and regulator remits may not effectively mitigate risks posed by highly capable general-purpose AI systems. Many regulators in UK can struggle to enforce existing rules on those actors designing, training, and developing most powerful general-purpose AI systems. It is not always clear how existing rules can be applied to effectively address risks that highly capable general-purpose models can present. Existing rules and laws are frequently applied to deployment or application level of AI, but organizations deploying or using these systems may not be well placed to identify, assess, or mitigate risks they can present. If this is case, new responsibilities on developers of highly capable general-purpose models may more effectively address risks. The government's ongoing work analysing life cycle accountability for AI may eventually need to consider role of other actors across value chain, such as data or cloud hosting providers, to determine how legal responsibility for AI may be distributed most fairly and effectively. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 07.1
Title: Development Phase: Developer Actions to Address Risks

During design and development of general-purpose foundation models, responsibility rests with developers. Developers should implement certification or training for programmers involved in AI development. They should conduct data protection impact assessments before training LMMs. Training data should be collected with best-practice data protection rules and should be refreshed, up-to-date and context-appropriate. Developers should ensure transparency of training data including sources and characteristics. They should ensure fair wages and support to data workers responsible for annotation and content filtering. Developers should involve diverse stakeholders in design process and design for accuracy and predictability. They should design to improve energy efficiency of models and implement security controls including securing model weights. Developers should establish reporting structures for vulnerabilities.

SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 3.2 Safe
SECTION: 3.2 Safe
TOPIC: How AI systems should be designed and operated to ensure safety, including practices for responsible development, clear information, and alignment with established safety guidelines.
---
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life, health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe operation of AI systems is improved through:

- responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
- clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;
- responsible decision-making by deployers and end users; and
- explanations and documentation of risks based on empirical evidence of incidents.

Different types of safety risks may require tailored AI risk management approaches based on context and the severity of potential risks presented. Safety risks that pose a potential risk of serious injury or death call for the most urgent prioritization and most thorough risk management process.

Employing safety considerations during the lifecycle and starting as early as possible with planning and design can prevent failures or conditions that can render a system dangerous. Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality.

AI safety risk management approaches should take cues from efforts and guidelines for safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or application-specific guidelines or standards. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.05
Title: Highly Capable AI: Emerging Safety Processes Framework

Ahead of AI Safety Summit, UK government outlined set of emerging safety processes to provide information to companies on ensuring and maintaining safety of AI technologies. Document covers nine emerging processes: (1) Responsible Capability Scaling - framework for managing risk as organizations scale capability of frontier AI systems; (2) Model Evaluations and Red Teaming - methods to assess risks AI systems pose; (3) Model Reporting and Information Sharing - practices that increase government visibility of frontier AI development and deployment; (4) Security Controls including Securing Model Weights - measures such as cyber security that underpin AI system security; (5) Reporting Structure for Vulnerabilities - process to enable outsiders to identify safety and security issues; (6) Identifiers of AI-generated Material - tools to mitigate creation and distribution of deceptive AI-generated content; (7) Prioritising Research on Risks Posed by AI; (8) Preventing and Monitoring Model Misuse; (9) Data Input Controls and Audits - measures to identify and manage training data that is likely to increase dangerous capabilities. SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 1.4a
Title- PRINCIPLE 1.4a: ROBUSTNESS, SECURITY AND SAFETY - CORE REQUIREMENTS

AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks. This requires comprehensive testing, validation, and ongoing monitoring to ensure AI systems behave as intended and remain safe across a range of operating conditions and potential misuse scenarios.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 3.2 Safe
SECTION: 3.2 Safe
TOPIC: How AI systems should be designed and operated to ensure safety, including practices for responsible development, clear information, and alignment with established safety guidelines.
---
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life, health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe operation of AI systems is improved through:

- responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
- clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;
- responsible decision-making by deployers and end users; and
- explanations and documentation of risks based on empirical evidence of incidents.

Different types of safety risks may require tailored AI risk management approaches based on context and the severity of potential risks presented. Safety risks that pose a potential risk of serious injury or death call for the most urgent prioritization and most thorough risk management process.

Employing safety considerations during the lifecycle and starting as early as possible with planning and design can prevent failures or conditions that can render a system dangerous. Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality.

AI safety risk management approaches should take cues from efforts and guidelines for safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or application-specific guidelines or standards. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.05
Title: Highly Capable AI: Emerging Safety Processes Framework

Ahead of AI Safety Summit, UK government outlined set of emerging safety processes to provide information to companies on ensuring and maintaining safety of AI technologies. Document covers nine emerging processes: (1) Responsible Capability Scaling - framework for managing risk as organizations scale capability of frontier AI systems; (2) Model Evaluations and Red Teaming - methods to assess risks AI systems pose; (3) Model Reporting and Information Sharing - practices that increase government visibility of frontier AI development and deployment; (4) Security Controls including Securing Model Weights - measures such as cyber security that underpin AI system security; (5) Reporting Structure for Vulnerabilities - process to enable outsiders to identify safety and security issues; (6) Identifiers of AI-generated Material - tools to mitigate creation and distribution of deceptive AI-generated content; (7) Prioritising Research on Risks Posed by AI; (8) Preventing and Monitoring Model Misuse; (9) Data Input Controls and Audits - measures to identify and manage training data that is likely to increase dangerous capabilities. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 5.2
Title: Human Alternatives: Fallback and Escalation Process

You should have access to timely human consideration and remedy by a fallback and escalation process if an automated system fails, it produces an error, or you would like to appeal or contest its impacts on you. Human consideration and fallback should be accessible, equitable, effective, maintained, accompanied by appropriate operator training, and should not impose an unreasonable burden on the public.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.1.19
Title: Misuse Risks: Preventing Malicious Use of AI Technologies

AI capabilities may be used maliciously, for example, to perform cyberattacks or design weapons. Developments in AI can amplify existing risks by enabling less sophisticated threat actors to carry out more substantial attacks at larger scale. The government is working with industry, academia, and international partners to find proportionate, practical mitigations to these risks. The 2023 refreshed Biological Security Strategy will ensure that by 2030 UK is resilient to spectrum of biological risks and world leader in responsible innovation. Some risks presented by AI systems are manifesting today as these technologies are misused to increase scale, speed, and success of criminal offences. In order to address potential criminal use of AI, the government is reviewing extent to which existing criminal law provides coverage of AI-enabled offending and harmful behaviour. The government will make amendments to existing legal frameworks as required to protect law and order. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 05.6
Title: Health System Risk: Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities

As health-care systems become increasingly dependent on AI, technologies could be targeted for malicious attacks and hacking and some systems shut down, with manipulation of data used to train algorithm, thereby changing its performance and recommendations, or data could be kidnapped for ransom. Particular security risk is feeding of sensitive data into LMMs that are not protected from unauthorized disclosure or use. LMMs themselves may also be vulnerable to cyber-security risks such as prompt injection, which is attack in which data are fed to LMM by third party. Cybersecurity vulnerabilities represent critical threat to patient safety, data integrity and health system operations. Malicious attacks could compromise clinical decision-making, expose sensitive patient information and disrupt essential health services.

Title- PRINCIPLE 1.4a: ROBUSTNESS, SECURITY AND SAFETY - CORE REQUIREMENTS

AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks. Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility.

SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 06.1
Title: AI Value Chain: Development, Provision and Deployment Stages

LMMs can be considered products of series of decisions on programming and product development by one or more actors. Decisions made at each stage of AI value chain may have both direct and indirect consequences on those who participate in development, deployment and use of LMMs downstream. AI value chain begins with integration of several inputs comprising AI infrastructure such as data, computing power and AI expertise to development of general-purpose foundation models. General-purpose foundation model can be used by third party (provider) through active programming interface for specific purpose. Provider can market product or service based on LMM to customer (deployer) such as ministry of health, health-care system, hospital or pharmaceutical company. Value chain can be vertically integrated so that company that collects data and trains model can also provide application directly to users.
 SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 07.1
Title: Development Phase: Developer Actions to Address Risks

During design and development of general-purpose foundation models, responsibility rests with developers. Developers should implement certification or training for programmers involved in AI development. They should conduct data protection impact assessments before training LMMs. Training data should be collected with best-practice data protection rules and should be refreshed, up-to-date and context-appropriate. Developers should ensure transparency of training data including sources and characteristics. They should ensure fair wages and support to data workers responsible for annotation and content filtering. Developers should involve diverse stakeholders in design process and design for accuracy and predictability. They should design to improve energy efficiency of models and implement security controls including securing model weights. Developers should establish reporting structures for vulnerabilities.
 SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.2.05
Title: Highly Capable AI: Emerging Safety Processes Framework

Ahead of AI Safety Summit, UK government outlined set of emerging safety processes to provide information to companies on ensuring and maintaining safety of AI technologies. Document covers nine emerging processes: (1) Responsible Capability Scaling - framework for managing risk as organizations scale capability of frontier AI systems; (2) Model Evaluations and Red Teaming - methods to assess risks AI systems pose; (3) Model Reporting and Information Sharing - practices that increase government visibility of frontier AI development and deployment; (4) Security Controls including Securing Model Weights - measures such as cyber security that underpin AI system security; (5) Reporting Structure for Vulnerabilities - process to enable outsiders to identify safety and security issues; (6) Identifiers of AI-generated Material - tools to mitigate creation and distribution of deceptive AI-generated content; (7) Prioritising Research on Risks Posed by AI; (8) Preventing and Monitoring Model Misuse; (9) Data Input Controls and Audits - measures to identify and manage training data that is likely to increase dangerous capabilities.

Four distinct deficiencies exist in the current submission for this control:

1. **DPIA absence**: No Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) has been conducted or referenced in relation to the adoption of the pre-trained GPT-4o model, as required by WHO guidance Section 07.1. The submission contains no evidence that privacy risks introduced by the upstream model were formally assessed prior to or alongside deployment.

2. **Training data provenance gap**: The submission references Microsoft's transparency documentation but provides no summary or extract of what that documentation actually covers. Key characteristics of GPT-4o's training data — including data sources, filtering methods, known limitations, and bias considerations — are entirely absent from the submission record.

3. **Vulnerability reporting structure missing**: There is no reference to any process or structure for reporting, escalating, or tracking safety and security vulnerabilities identified in the pre-trained model supply chain, as required under UK AI Regulation Section 5.2.05, point 5. Neither an internal escalation path nor an external disclosure channel (e.g., to Microsoft/OpenAI) is described.

4. **No periodic review cadence defined**: Beyond the initial April 2026 approval, the submission does not specify any scheduled review cycle for the licensing agreement or model transparency documentation. There is no commitment to re-evaluate these artefacts as the model, its licensing terms, or the regulatory landscape evolves.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap in sequence before the Certifier phase:

1. **DPIA**: Conduct and document a formal DPIA scoped to the GPT-4o model adoption. The DPIA should assess data flows into and out of the model, identify privacy risks (e.g., training data memorisation, inference risks), and record mitigations and the sign-off authority. Reference WHO guidance Section 07.1 explicitly in the DPIA document.

2. **Training data provenance summary**: Retrieve and review Microsoft's published transparency documentation for GPT-4o. Produce an internal summary artefact (minimum one page) that captures: training data sources and date ranges, known exclusions or filters applied, identified biases or limitations, and any third-party audits referenced. Attach this summary — alongside a link or copy of the source documentation — to the submission.

3. **Vulnerability reporting structure**: Define and document a vulnerability reporting process covering: (a) an internal channel for staff to flag suspected model safety/security issues; (b) a named responsible owner for triage; (c) an escalation path to Microsoft/OpenAI via their responsible disclosure programme; and (d) a target response/resolution SLA. Embed this process within the existing AI risk or incident management SOP, and cross-reference UK AI Regulation Section 5.2.05, point 5.

4. **Periodic review cadence**: Amend the governance documentation to specify a formal review schedule — recommended minimum annually, or triggered by: a new model version release, a material change to the licensing agreement, a significant regulatory update, or a security incident. Assign a named role responsible for initiating each review and record the outcome in a review log.

SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 2.1.00
Title: Executive Summary: AI Progress and Benefits

The pace of progress in Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been unlike any previous technology. Benefits are already being realised across the UK: AI is helping make jobs safer and more satisfying, conserve wildlife, fight climate change, and make public services more efficient. The UK must plan for capabilities and uses of AI systems today, while preparing for a near future where the most powerful systems are broadly accessible and significantly more capable. The UK is investing more in AI safety than any other country in the world. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.2
Title: Applications: Scientific and Medical Research

LMMs are extending ways in which AI can support scientific and medical research. They can generate text to be used in scientific article, for submitting manuscripts or in writing peer review. They can be used to summarize texts including summaries for academic papers or can generate abstracts. LMMs can be used to analyse and summarize data to gain new insights in clinical and scientific research. They can be used to edit text, improving grammar, readability and conciseness of written documents such as articles and grant proposals. LMMs can be used to gain insights from data with which it was trained. One LMM trained on millions of academic articles is claimed to be able to analyse scientific research to answer questions, extract information or generate relevant text. However, concerns include lack of accountability, high-income country bias, hallucination and misinformation, and undermining of trust in peer review process. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 04.1
Title: LMM Applications: Patient-Centered Uses and Self-Care

LMMs could accelerate trend towards use of AI by patients and laypeople for medical purposes. Individuals have used Internet searches to obtain medical information for two decades. LMMs could play central role in providing information to patients and laypeople, including by integrating them into Internet searches. LMM-powered chatbots could serve as highly personalized, broadly focused virtual health assistants that leverage individual profiles to promote behaviour change, answer health-related questions, triage symptoms, or communicate with healthcare providers when appropriate. Specific LMM-powered chatbots could provide treatment in mental health. LMMs could also be used for identifying clinical trials or for enrolment in such trials, lowering cost of recruitment and increasing speed and efficiency.

SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 05.2
Title: Health System Risk: Accessibility and Affordability Barriers

Several factors can undermine equitable access to LMMs. Digital divide limits use of digital tools to certain countries, regions or segments of population. Digital divide leads to other disparities, many of which affect use of AI, and AI itself can reinforce and exacerbate disparity. Unlike Internet, many LMMs are available only by paying fee or subscription. It has been estimated that Chat GPT costs US$ 700,000 per day to operate. Some companies are introducing subscription fees for new versions of LMMs, which could make certain LMMs unaffordable in low- and middle-income countries and for individuals, health systems or local governments in resource-poor settings. Poor people could be limited to using LMMs as cost-effective solution while access to real health-care professionals limited to wealthier individuals. Most LMMs operate only in English.
 SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 7.3
Title: Definition: Equity

"Equity" means the consistent and systematic fair, just, and impartial treatment of all individuals. Systemic, fair, and just treatment must take into account the status of individuals who belong to underserved communities that have been denied such treatment, such as Black, Latino, and Indigenous and Native American persons, Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders and other persons of color; members of religious minorities; women, girls, and non-binary people; lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and intersex (LGBTQI+) persons; older adults; persons with disabilities; persons who live in rural areas; and persons otherwise adversely affected by persistent poverty or inequality. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 2.4
Title: Algorithmic Discrimination: Proactive Equity Assessment

Those responsible for the development, use, or oversight of automated systems should conduct proactive equity assessments in the design phase of the technology research and development or during its acquisition to review potential input data, associated historical context, accessibility for people with disabilities, and societal goals to identify potential discrimination and effects on equity resulting from the introduction of the technology. The assessed groups should be as inclusive as possible of the underserved communities: Black, Latino, and Indigenous and Native American persons, Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders and other persons of color; members of religious minorities; women, girls, and non-binary people; LGBTQI+ persons; older adults; persons with disabilities; persons who live in rural areas.

Context: StudySpark AI is a staff-facing internal tool. Students do not access it directly, so
student-facing equity concerns around cost, language, or device access do not apply to the
tool itself.
Staff equity: All seven LSO staff have equal access via the same SSO-gated portal on
university-provided devices. No staff member faces a cost, language, or infrastructure

Indirect equity consideration: Because the tool may help staff respond to students more

gap_description.what_is_missing:
Five compounding equity gaps are present in this submission:

1. **No proactive equity assessment at design/acquisition phase** — There is no documented structured review of input data, historical context, or discriminatory effects on underserved groups, as required by the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (Section 2.4). The submission offers only a generic policy statement with no substantive analysis.

2. **Language accessibility not addressed** — The submission does not evaluate whether non-native English-speaking staff face usability barriers when interacting with the tool, which is a material concern given WHO guidance on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) operating predominantly in English.

3. **Disability-related accessibility for staff users not assessed** — There is no documented consideration of screen reader compatibility, cognitive accessibility of the interface, or other assistive technology requirements for staff users with disabilities — a dimension explicitly required by the control.

4. **Indirect equity impact on students not systematically assessed** — While indirect effects on students are acknowledged, no documented analysis exists of whether the tool's outputs could differentially affect student subgroups (e.g., students with disabilities, students from minority or linguistically diverse backgrounds).

5. **Cost and affordability sustainability not considered** — There is no reference to affordability or cost sustainability at the organisational level, including contingency planning if institutional licensing arrangements change, which could create future access inequities.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap in sequence before the Certifier phase:

1. **Equity Assessment Document (Design/Acquisition Phase):** Produce a structured equity impact assessment covering: (a) review of any training or input data for representational bias; (b) historical context of the tool's deployment domain; (c) identification of underserved or at-risk groups among both staff and student populations. Map findings explicitly to Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights Section 2.4 requirements.

2. **Language Accessibility Review:** Conduct and document a language accessibility audit of the tool's interface and outputs. Identify whether non-English-speaking staff are disadvantaged in usability, and specify any mitigations (e.g., multilingual support, translated guidance materials, workflow accommodations). Reference WHO LMM guidance in the rationale.

3. **Disability Accessibility Assessment for Staff:** Commission or document a technical accessibility review of the tool's interface against recognised standards (e.g., WCAG 2.1 AA), covering screen reader compatibility, keyboard navigation, and cognitive accessibility. Record findings and any remediation steps or compensating controls.

4. **Student Subgroup Impact Analysis:** Produce a documented analysis — even if qualitative — of how the tool's outputs could differentially affect student subgroups. Include students with disabilities and students from minority or linguistically diverse backgrounds. Where quantitative data is unavailable, use structured expert judgement and document assumptions.

5. **Cost Sustainability Statement:** Append a brief affordability and cost sustainability section to the equity assessment, addressing: current licensing model, risk of access disruption if licensing changes, and any contingency or equity safeguard measures in place.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 1.30
Title- PRINCIPLE 1.30: TRANSPARENCY AND EXPLAINABILITY

AI Actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure regarding AI systems. To this end, they should provide meaningful information, appropriate to the context, and consistent with the state of art: (i) to foster a general understanding of AI systems, including their capabilities and limitations, (ii) to make stakeholders aware of their interactions with AI systems, including in the workplace, (iii) where feasible and useful, to provide plain and easy-to-understand information on the sources of data/input, factors, processes and/or logic that led to the prediction, content, recommendation or decision, to enable those affected by an AI system to understand the output, and (iv) to provide information that enable those adversely affected by an AI system to challenge its output. SOURCE: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence | Section III.2.7
Title: PRINCIPLE7 TRANSPARENCY AND EXPLAINABILITY

AI systems should be as transparent and explainable as possible. Organizations should provide clear information about how AI systems work, their capabilities, limitations, and potential risks. The level of transparency and explainability required should be proportional to the risks and impacts of the system. Users and affected individuals should be able to understand the logic behind AI-driven decisions that affect them. Documentation should be maintained throughout the AI system's development and deployment. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility.

gap_description.what_is_missing:
Three distinct deficiencies are present in this submission for the User-facing disclosure control under P6:

1. **Challenge/Query Mechanism (OECD 1.30(iv))**: There is no documented mechanism enabling students or affected individuals to contest, query, or seek human review of AI-influenced outputs. The submission makes no reference to a redress pathway, escalation route, or point of contact for challenging AI decisions.

2. **Privacy Notice Content Unverifiable**: The privacy notice is referenced but neither reproduced nor meaningfully summarised. The adequacy of its AI disclosure language — including whether it meets the specificity required for a PG assurance level — cannot be independently assessed from the submission as provided.

3. **Ongoing Monitoring & Audit of Disclosure Practices**: There is no articulation of how disclosure practices are monitored, reviewed, or audited over time. The June 2026 ownership date is noted, but no periodic review cadence, audit trigger, or compliance assurance mechanism is described beyond that single milestone.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap as follows before the Certifier phase:

1. **Challenge/Query Mechanism**: Draft and publish a documented redress procedure that explicitly grants students and affected individuals the right to query or challenge AI-influenced outputs. This should name a responsible role (e.g., Academic Registrar, AI Governance Lead), define the submission channel (e.g., form, email alias), set a response SLA, and reference the escalation path to human review. Cross-reference this procedure in the privacy notice and any student-facing AI disclosure materials.

2. **Privacy Notice Content**: Reproduce or provide a verbatim extract (or a structured summary) of the current privacy notice's AI disclosure section within the submission. The extract must demonstrate that it: (a) identifies that AI is used, (b) describes the nature and purpose of AI involvement, (c) explains the implications for the individual, and (d) signposts the challenge/query mechanism. If the notice is inadequate, revise it and resubmit the updated version.

3. **Monitoring & Audit Cadence**: Define and document a recurring review schedule for disclosure practices (e.g., annual review, triggered review upon system change or regulatory update). Specify who is responsible for conducting the review, what criteria are assessed, and how findings are recorded and acted upon. Evidence of at least one completed review cycle, or a formally approved review plan with scheduled dates, should be provided.

reviewer_records.rag_context:
SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 1.4a
Title- PRINCIPLE 1.4a: ROBUSTNESS, SECURITY AND SAFETY - CORE REQUIREMENTS

AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks. This requires comprehensive testing, validation, and ongoing monitoring to ensure AI systems behave as intended and remain safe across a range of operating conditions and potential misuse scenarios. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education.

SOURCE: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence | Section III.2.7
Title: PRINCIPLE7 TRANSPARENCY AND EXPLAINABILITY

AI systems should be as transparent and explainable as possible. Organizations should provide clear information about how AI systems work, their capabilities, limitations, and potential risks. The level of transparency and explainability required should be proportional to the risks and impacts of the system. Users and affected individuals should be able to understand the logic behind AI-driven decisions that affect them. Documentation should be maintained throughout the AI system's development and deployment. SOURCE: OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence | Section 1.30
Title- PRINCIPLE 1.30: TRANSPARENCY AND EXPLAINABILITY

AI Actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure regarding AI systems. To this end, they should provide meaningful information, appropriate to the context, and consistent with the state of art: (i) to foster a general understanding of AI systems, including their capabilities and limitations, (ii) to make stakeholders aware of their interactions with AI systems, including in the workplace, (iii) where feasible and useful, to provide plain and easy-to-understand information on the sources of data/input, factors, processes and/or logic that led to the prediction, content, recommendation or decision, to enable those affected by an AI system to understand the output, and (iv) to provide information that enable those adversely affected by an AI system to challenge its output. SOURCE: Nist.Ai.100 1 | 3.5 Explainable and Interpretable
SECTION: 3.5 Explainable and Interpretable
TOPIC: The definitions of explainability and interpretability in AI, how they provide insights into system functionality and trustworthiness, and their distinct relationship with transparency.
---
Explainability refers to a representation of the mechanisms underlying AI systems’ operation, whereas interpretability refers to the meaning of AI systems’ output in the context of their designed functional purposes. Together, explainability and interpretability assist those operating or overseeing an AI system, as well as users of an AI system, to gain deeper insights into the functionality and trustworthiness of the system, including its outputs. The underlying assumption is that perceptions of negative risk stem from a lack of ability to make sense of, or contextualize, system output appropriately. Explainable and interpretable AI systems offer information that will help end users understand the purposes and potential impact of an AI system.

Risk from lack of explainability may be managed by describing how AI systems function, with descriptions tailored to individual differences such as the user’s role, knowledge, and skill level. Explainable systems can be debugged and monitored more easily, and they lend themselves to more thorough documentation, audit, and governance.

Risks to interpretability often can be addressed by communicating a description of why an AI system made a particular prediction or recommendation. (See “Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence” and “Psychological Foundations of Explainability and Interpretability in Artificial Intelligence” found here.)

Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are distinct characteristics that support each other. Transparency can answer the question of “what happened” in the system. Explainability can answer the question of “how” a decision was made in the system. Interpretability can answer the question of “why” a decision was made by the system and its meaning or context to the user.

gap_description.what_is_missing:
Three distinct explainability gaps are present in the submission for Control P6 (Explainability appropriate to context — technical and user):

1. **Challenge/Query Pathway**: There is no documented mechanism enabling staff to escalate or formally query the AI's rationale beyond a one-line note. The OECD principle requires that affected parties can meaningfully challenge AI outputs, and the current submission does not describe any lightweight escalation path, feedback loop, or query resolution process to support this.

2. **Ongoing Explainability Maintenance**: There is no description of how the explainability mechanism (e.g., the one-line rationale) is reviewed, re-validated, or updated when the underlying model, prompting approach, or system configuration changes. Without a review cadence or change-triggered re-validation process, explainability adequacy cannot be assured over time.

3. **Technical-Layer Explainability**: The submission addresses explainability only for operational staff. There is no coverage of explainability for system administrators, developers, or auditors — the technical audience explicitly referenced in the control title. This leaves the 'technical' dimension of the control materially unaddressed at the PG assurance level.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion:
Address each gap with the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase:

1. **Challenge/Query Pathway**: Define and document a lightweight escalation process that allows staff to formally query or challenge an AI-generated rationale. This should specify: who receives the query (e.g., a nominated AI system owner or team lead), the expected response timeframe, how outcomes are recorded, and how repeated challenges inform model or prompt review. Embed this pathway in the relevant operational SOP or staff-facing guidance.

2. **Explainability Maintenance**: Establish and document a review trigger and cadence for the explainability mechanism. At minimum, specify that any change to the model version, prompting approach, or output format triggers a re-validation of the one-line rationale mechanism's adequacy. Include this as a standing item in the system's change management or model governance process, and record outcomes in a version-controlled log.

3. **Technical-Layer Explainability**: Produce a technical explainability document targeting system administrators, developers, and auditors. This should describe: how the AI generates outputs (e.g., model type, prompting architecture, inference pipeline), what logging and traceability mechanisms exist at the system level, how auditors can reconstruct or inspect a decision trace, and what monitoring or alerting is in place. This artefact should be distinct from operational staff guidance and referenced in the system's technical documentation suite.

SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 11
TITLE: Technical documentation

Providers of high-risk AI systems shall draw up technical documentation that demonstrates compliance with the requirements of this Regulation. The technical documentation shall include a general description of the AI system, the intended purpose, the training and testing procedures used. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 14.1
Title: Applications: Clerical Functions and Administrative Tasks

LMMs are being used to assist health professionals in clerical, administrative and financial aspects of practising medicine. Medicine exposes physicians and other health-care professionals to ever-growing paperwork for numerous obligations for recording patient information and data in electronic health records, billing and other administrative tasks. Documentation constituted one fourth to one half of doctor's time and one fifth of nurse's time. LMMs have been singled out as means of returning time to health-care professionals to reduce burn-out and allocate more time to providing care. Examples of uses include better communication to assist in translation, to fill in missing information in electronic health records, and to draft clinical notes after each patient visit. However, serious errors could arise due to inaccuracies, mistakes or hallucinations. LMMs can be inconsistent with slight changes to prompt generating completely different electronic health record. SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 50
TITLE: Documentation requirements

All documentation required under this Regulation shall be:
(a) kept in an easily accessible form;
(b) in an official language of the Member State or English;
(c) regularly updated to reflect changes in the AI system;
(d) retained for the period specified in this Regulation or as required by other applicable laws.

SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 17
TITLE: Monitoring and logging

Users of high-risk AI systems shall monitor the operation of the AI system and keep logs of its outputs. Users shall ensure that the AI system is not used beyond its intended purpose and shall report any malfunctioning or degraded performance to the provider. SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 14.1
Title: Applications: Clerical Functions and Administrative Tasks

LMMs are being used to assist health professionals in clerical, administrative and financial aspects of practising medicine. Medicine exposes physicians and other health-care professionals to ever-growing paperwork for numerous obligations for recording patient information and data in electronic health records, billing and other administrative tasks. Documentation constituted one fourth to one half of doctor's time and one fifth of nurse's time. LMMs have been singled out as means of returning time to health-care professionals to reduce burn-out and allocate more time to providing care. Examples of uses include better communication to assist in translation, to fill in missing information in electronic health records, and to draft clinical notes after each patient visit. However, serious errors could arise due to inaccuracies, mistakes or hallucinations. LMMs can be inconsistent with slight changes to prompt generating completely different electronic health record. SOURCE: EU AI Act | Article 9
TITLE: Logging, documentation and record-keeping

Providers of high-risk AI systems shall implement technical and organisational measures to ensure that the operation of their AI systems is logged and documented. The logs shall be kept for a period of at least 30 months after the AI system has been placed on the market or put into service.

gap_description.what_is_missing: Five distinct logging and accountability deficiencies are present: (1) Raw prompt inputs are not retained post-session — while privacy-motivated, this eliminates any retrospective audit capability for error, complaint, or malfunction investigations as required under EU AI Act Article 17; (2) AI-generated draft outputs are not logged or stored — only the final sent message is captured, making it impossible to review edited or discarded AI-generated content for quality failures, hallucinations, or misuse; (3) No log retention period is defined — EU AI Act Article 9 mandates logs be kept for a minimum of 30 months after the system is placed in service, and no such commitment or mechanism is documented; (4) No mechanism exists for detecting or reporting AI malfunctioning or degraded performance to the provider, as explicitly required by EU AI Act Article 17; (5) There is no description of how logging supports detection of use beyond the system's intended purpose, leaving out-of-scope or adversarial use invisible to operators.
gap_description.actionable_suggestion: Take the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase: (1) INPUT RETENTION — Design and implement a privacy-preserving input logging mechanism (e.g., pseudonymised or hashed prompt records) that retains sufficient audit-relevant metadata (timestamp, session ID, user role, input category) even where full prompt text is not stored; document the privacy-vs-accountability trade-off decision in a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) or equivalent record; (2) DRAFT OUTPUT LOGGING — Extend the logging pipeline to capture all AI-generated outputs at the point of generation, not only the final sent message; tag each log entry with a 'draft' or 'final' flag and a diff-indicator where edits occurred, enabling retrospective quality and misuse review; (3) RETENTION SCHEDULE — Define and document a formal log retention policy specifying a minimum 30-month retention period aligned with EU AI Act Article 9; include storage location, access controls, deletion procedures, and the date the system was placed in service as the retention start anchor; (4) MALFUNCTION REPORTING — Implement and document a mechanism for detecting degraded or anomalous AI performance (e.g., latency thresholds, output error-rate monitoring, user-flagging workflow) and define a clear escalation and provider-notification procedure; assign a named responsible role for triggering reports; (5) INTENDED-PURPOSE BOUNDARY DETECTION — Define the system's intended-use boundary in logging terms (e.g., permitted task categories, user roles, input patterns) and configure log-based alerting or periodic review to flag interactions that fall outside those boundaries; document how findings feed into the incident management process.

SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 13.1
Title: Applications: Medical and Nursing Education

LMMs are projected to play role in medical and nursing education. They could be used to create dynamic texts that, in comparison with generic texts, are tailored to specific needs and questions of student. LMMs integrated into chatbots can provide simulated conversations to improve clinician-patient communication and problem-solving including practising medical interviewing, diagnostic reasoning and explaining treatment options. Chatbot could be tailored to provide student with various virtual patients including those with disabilities or rare medical conditions. LMMs could provide instruction in which medical student asks questions and receives responses accompanied by reasoning through chain-of-thought including physiological and biological processes. However, use of AI can also pose risk that professionals suspend their judgement in favour of computer. If LMM provides incorrect information or fabricates response, it could affect quality of medical education. SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 8.3
Title: Examples: Education-Related Automated Systems

Education-related systems such as algorithms that purport to detect student cheating or plagiarism, admissions algorithms, online or virtual reality student environments, educational technology platforms, and any system that has the meaningful potential to impact equal opportunities including equitable access to education. These systems should be designed with consideration for student privacy, fairness, and accessibility. SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 2.4.00
Title: Executive Summary: AI Safety Institute Establishment

The AI Safety Institute was created to lead evaluations and safety research in UK government, in collaboration with international partners including the US. At the AI Safety Summit, leading AI developers committed to sharing the most powerful AI models with governments for testing to ensure safety today and prepare for risks of tomorrow. The Institute will conduct pre- and post-deployment testing of the most powerful AI systems, performing evaluations to characterize safety-relevant capabilities, understand safety and security of systems, and assess societal impacts.
